title: 1.2 Variables and constants
text: A variable is a named box in memory. You choose the name, the compiler chooses the address. int age = 20; // variable: value can change const float PI = 3.14159f; // constant: compiler blocks changes #define MAX_USERS 50 // macro: text replaced before compiling age = 21; // fine // PI = 3.14; // ERROR: assignment of read-only variable

title: 1.3 What is a data type?
text: A data type tells the compiler (1) how much memory to reserve, (2) how to read the bits stored there, and (3) which operations are allowed. Analogy: boxes with labels Memory is a warehouse of boxes. The type is the box size plus a label. The bits 01000001 mean the number 65 if the label says int, and the letter A if the label says char. title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is a data type? It defines the size, interpretation and allowed operations of a variable. Q2. What are the stages of compilation? Preprocessing, compiling, assembling, linking. Q3. Difference between const and #define? const creates a typed variable that the compiler protects; #define is plain text replacement before compiling and has no type. Q4. Why is sizeof(int) not always 4? The standard only sets a minimum (16 bits); the real size depends on the processor and compiler. Q5. What does void main() vs int main() mean? The standard form is int main(void), returning a status to the OS. void main is non-standard on hosted systems, though common in bare-metal code. TOPIC 2

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. Difference between ++a and a++? Pre-increment adds 1 then uses the value; post-increment uses the value then adds 1. Q2. Difference between while and do-while? do-while checks the condition after the body, so it always runs at least once. Q3. What is short-circuit evaluation? In a && b, b is skipped if a is false; in a || b, b is skipped if a is true. Q4. What happens if you forget break in switch? Execution falls through into the next case. Q5. Why do embedded programs use while(1)? There is no OS to return to, so main loops forever handling tasks. TOPIC 3

title: 3.3 Call by value
text: C passes copies of the arguments. Changing the parameter inside the function does not change the original variable. void bad_swap(int a, int b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; // swaps only the copies } int x = 1, y = 2; bad_swap(x, y); printf("%d %d\n", x, y); // still 1 2 Output: 1 2 To change the original you pass its address (a pointer). That is the swap fix in Topic 5.

title: 3.5 Recursion
text: A recursive function must have (1) a base case that stops the recursion and (2) a recursive case that moves toward the base case. unsigned long factorial(unsigned int n) { if (n <= 1) // base case return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive case } Trace of factorial(4) (calls go down, answers come back up): Call Waits for Returns factorial(4) 4 * factorial(3) 24 factorial(3) 3 * factorial(2) 6 factorial(2) 2 * factorial(1) 2 factorial(1) base case 1 Call Waits for Returns factorial(4) 4 * factorial(3) 24 factorial(3) 3 * factorial(2) 6 factorial(2) 2 * factorial(1) 2 factorial(1) base case 1

title: 3.6 What happens in memory: the stack
text: Every call pushes a stack frame (parameters, local variables, return address). When the function returns, the frame is removed. Deep recursion means many frames; run out of stack and the program crashes (stack overflow). Recursion on microcontrollers An ESP8266 or Uno has very little RAM and stack. Many embedded coding standards (MISRA) forbid recursion. Prefer loops in firmware; use recursion to learn and in tree or parsing problems on PCs. Prefer loops in firmware; use recursion to learn and in tree or parsing problems on PCs. int fib(int n) { // easy to read, but slow: it repeats work if (n < 2) return n; return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); } int fib_loop(int n) { // fast and uses constant stack int a = 0, b = 1; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int t = a + b; a = b; b = t; } return a; }

title: 3.7 Splitting code into files (header files)
text: // mathutil.h #ifndef MATHUTIL_H #define MATHUTIL_H int add(int a, int b); int max(int a, int b); #endif // mathutil.c #include "mathutil.h" int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int max(int a, int b) { return a > b ? a : b; } // main.c #include <stdio.h> #include "mathutil.h" int main(void) { printf("%d\n", add(2, 3)); return 0; } Build: gcc main.c mathutil.c -o app. The header is the public menu; the .c file is the kitchen.

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is call by value? The function receives copies of the arguments, so changes do not affect the originals. Q2. Difference between declaration and definition? A declaration tells the compiler the signature; the definition provides the body. Q3. What is a stack frame? The block of stack memory holding a call's parameters, locals and return address. Q4. What is the base case in recursion? The condition where the function stops calling itself. Q5. Why avoid recursion in firmware? Stack is small and usage is hard to predict; overflow causes a crash that is hard to debug. Q6. What does static do to a local variable? It keeps its value between calls and lives for the whole program. TOPIC 4

title: 4.1 One-dimensional arrays
text: Analogy: a row of lockers Lockers are numbered 0, 1, 2... All lockers are the same size and sit next to each other. The array name is the building; the index picks the locker. The array name is the building; the index picks the locker. int marks[5] = {90, 85, 70, 60, 95}; // 5 ints, 20 bytes on a 32-bit int system int zeros[5] = {0}; // all zeros int auto_size[] = {1, 2, 3}; // compiler counts: size 3 printf("%d\n", marks[0]); // 90 (first element) printf("%d\n", marks[4]); // 95 (last element) for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", marks[i]); int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]); // number of elements = 5

title: 4.2 Two-dimensional arrays
text: int m[2][3] = { {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6} }; // 2 rows, 3 columns for (int r = 0; r < 2; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) printf("%d ", m[r][c]); printf("\n"); } Output: 1 2 3 4 5 6 Memory is one long line; C stores rows one after another (row-major). So m[1][0] sits right after m[0][2].

title: 4.3 Passing arrays to functions
text: An array passed to a function becomes a pointer to its first element, so the function can change the original. The size is lost, so pass it separately. void print_array(const int arr[], int n) { // const: we only read it for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%d ", arr[i]); } int find_max(const int arr[], int n) { int max = arr[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) if (arr[i] > max) max = arr[i]; return max; }

title: 4.4 Searching and sorting
text: // Bubble sort: repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order void bubble_sort(int a[], int n) { for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) { int t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; } } After pass 1 the largest element has "bubbled" to the end; after pass 2 the second largest is in place, and so on. Fine for learning; real code uses qsort or better algorithms.

title: 4.7 Writing your own strlen and reverse

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. Why do arrays start at index 0? The index is an offset from the first element: address = base + index x size. Q2. What is the null terminator? The character '\0' (value 0) that marks the end of a C string. Q3. sizeof("hello") vs strlen("hello")? sizeof is 6 (includes \0); strlen is 5. Q4. Does C check array bounds? No. Out-of-range access is undefined behaviour. Q5. Difference between char s[] = "hi" and char *s = "hi"? The first is a modifiable array copy; the second points to a read-only literal. Q6. How is a 2D array stored in memory? Row by row, in one contiguous block (row-major order). TOPIC 5

title: Pointers
text: In one line A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Pointers let functions change the caller's data, walk through arrays, and talk directly to hardware. title: 5.2 Pointer size
text: A pointer holds an address, so its size depends on the machine, not on what it points to: 8 bytes on 64-bit PCs, 4 bytes on ESP32, ESP8266 and ARM Cortex-M, 2 bytes on 8-bit AVR (Arduino Uno).

title: 5.3 Call by reference: the swap that works
text: void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; } int x = 1, y = 2; swap(&x, &y); printf("%d %d\n", x, y); // 2 1 Output: 2 1 C still passes by value, but the value passed is an address, so the function can reach the original. Functions that must return more than one result also use pointers (output parameters).

title: 5.4 Pointer arithmetic
text:
Adding 1 to a pointer moves it by one element, not one byte. For int *p, p + 1 adds sizeof(int) to the address. int arr[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40}; int *p = arr; // array name = address of first element printf("%d
", *p); // 10 printf("%d
", *(p + 2)); // 30 p++; // now points to arr[1] printf("%d
", *p); // 20 // arr[i] is exactly the same as *(arr + i)

title: 5.8 Function pointers
text: A function also lives at an address. A function pointer stores it, so you can choose which function to call at run time (callbacks, state machines, driver tables). int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int sub(int a, int b) { return a - b; } int (*op)(int, int); // op = pointer to function(int,int) returning int op = add; printf("%d\n", op(5, 3)); // 8 op = sub; printf("%d\n", op(5, 3)); // 2 Output: 8 2

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is a pointer? A variable that stores a memory address. Q2. Difference between * in a declaration and * in an expression? In int *p it means "p is a pointer"; in *p it means "the value at the address in p". Q3. What is a dangling pointer? A pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope. Q4. What is a void pointer? A generic pointer without a type; cast it before dereferencing. Q5. Difference between const int *p and int *const p? The first protects the data, the second protects the pointer itself. Q6. Why is arr[i] the same as *(arr + i)? The compiler defines indexing as pointer arithmetic: base address plus i elements. Q7. Where do you use function pointers in embedded code? Interrupt vector tables, callbacks, state machines and driver interfaces. TOPIC 6

title: Structures, Unions, Enums and typedef
text: In one line A struct groups different variables under one name, a union lets members share the same memory, an enum gives names to integer constants, and typedef gives a type a shorter name. In one line A struct groups different variables under one name, a union lets members share the same memory, an enum gives names to integer constants, and typedef gives a type a shorter name.

title: 6.1 Structures
text: Analogy: a form An array is a stack of identical sheets. A struct is one form with different fields: name, roll number, marks. One form describes one student. Analogy: a form An array is a stack of identical sheets. A struct is one form with different fields: name, roll number, marks. One form describes one student. struct Student { char name[20]; int roll; float marks; }; struct Student s1 = {"Ravi", 101, 88.5f}; struct Student s2; s2.roll = 102; // . accesses a member strcpy(s2.name, "Anu"); s2.marks = 91.0f; printf("%s %d %.1f\n", s1.name, s1.roll, s1.marks); Output: Ravi 101 88.5

title: 6.2 Pointers to structures and the arrow operator
text: Structures can be large. Passing a pointer avoids copying the whole struct, and the function can modify the original. Use -> with a pointer, . with a variable. void print_student(const struct Student *s) { printf("%s %d %.1f\n", s->name, s->roll, s->marks); // same as (*s).name } void give_bonus(struct Student *s) { s->marks += 5; } print_student(&s1); give_bonus(&s1);

title: 6.3 Array of structures
text: struct Student cls[3] = { {"Ravi", 101, 88.5f}, {"Anu", 102, 91.0f}, {"Kiran",103, 79.0f} }; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) printf("%d %s %.1f\n", cls[i].roll, cls[i].name, cls[i].marks);

title: 6.4 typedef: shorter names
text: typedef struct { float temperature; float humidity; uint32_t timestamp; } SensorData; SensorData reading = {27.5f, 60.0f, 1000}; // no need to write "struct" typedef does not create a new type; it just gives a new name. It is used everywhere in embedded code: uint8_t itself is a typedef.

title: 6.5 Struct padding and size
text: CPUs read memory fastest when a 4-byte int starts at an address divisible by 4. The compiler inserts unused padding bytes to keep members aligned, so sizeof(struct) can be bigger than the sum of its members. struct A { char a; int b; char c; }; // a, 3 pad, b (4), c, 3 pad -> 12 bytes struct B { int b; char a; char c; }; // b (4), a, c, 2 pad -> 8 bytes printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(struct A), sizeof(struct B)); // 12 8 Output: 12 8 Tip: list members from largest to smallest to save RAM. This matters when you have thousands of records on a microcontroller.

title: 6.6 Unions
text: In a union all members start at the same address. The size is that of the largest member, and only one member holds a meaningful value at a time. union Data { int i; float f; uint8_t bytes[4]; }; union Data d; d.f = 1.0f; printf("%02X %02X %02X %02X\n", d.bytes[0], d.bytes[1], d.bytes[2], d.bytes[3]); printf("%zu\n", sizeof(union Data)); Output: 00 00 80 3F 4 The output shows the four bytes of the float 1.0 (0x3F800000) on a little-endian machine, lowest byte first. Embedded uses of unions: viewing a 32-bit register as bytes or as bit fields, and sending different message types in one buffer. struct union Memory Each member has its own space Members share one space Size Sum of members + padding Size of the largest member Use Group related data Save memory, reinterpret the same bytes struct union Memory Each member has its own space Members share one space Size Sum of members + padding Size of the largest member Use Group related data Save memory, reinterpret the same bytes

title: 6.7 Enumerations
text: An enum gives readable names to integer constants. Values start at 0 and increase by 1 unless you set them. enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; // 0, 1, 2 enum State { IDLE = 10, RUNNING, ERROR }; // 10, 11, 12 enum Color c = GREEN; if (c == GREEN) printf("green = %d\n", c); // green = 1 Use enums for states in a state machine (Topic 18) instead of magic numbers like 0, 1, 2.

title: 6.8 Bit-fields
text: struct Flags { unsigned int power : 1; // 1 bit unsigned int mode : 2; // 2 bits (0 to 3) unsigned int error : 1; unsigned int : 4; // 4 unused bits }; struct Flags f = {0}; f.power = 1; f.mode = 2; Bit-fields are not portable The order of bits and the packing are decided by the compiler. title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. Difference between structure and union? Struct members have separate memory; union members share the same memory. Q2. What is structure padding? Unused bytes added so each member is aligned to its natural boundary for fast access. Q3. When do you use ->? To access a member through a pointer to a structure. Q4. What is typedef? A way to give a new name to an existing type. Q5. How can you reduce the size of a struct? Order members from large to small, or use packed attribute (with a speed or portability cost). Q6. What is an enum used for? Named integer constants, mainly states and options. TOPIC 7

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
text: In one line Dynamic memory lets a program request memory from the heap while it runs (malloc) and must give it back (free). On small microcontrollers it is usually avoided. In one line Dynamic memory lets a program request memory from the heap while it runs (malloc) and must give it back (free). On small microcontrollers it is usually avoided.

title: 7.1 Stack vs heap
text: Stack Heap Managed by Compiler (automatic) You (malloc / free) Holds Local variables, function calls Memory you request at run time Size known At compile time Decided while running Speed Very fast Slower Freed When the function returns When you call free Risk Stack overflow Leaks, fragmentation, dangling pointers Stack Heap Managed by Compiler (automatic) You (malloc / free) Holds Local variables, function calls Memory you request at run time Size known At compile time Decided while running Speed Very fast Slower Freed When the function returns When you call free Risk Stack overflow Leaks, fragmentation, dangling pointers Analogy: hotel rooms Stack is your own room that is cleaned automatically when you leave. Heap is renting a hall: you ask the manager (malloc), use it as long as you like, and must hand the keys back (free). If you forget, nobody else can use that hall. title: 7.2 The four functions (stdlib.h)
text: Function What it does malloc(size) Reserves size bytes; memory is NOT cleared; returns NULL on failure calloc(n, size) Reserves n x size bytes and sets all to zero realloc(ptr, size) Resizes a block (may move it); returns the new address free(ptr) Returns the block to the heap Function What it does malloc(size) Reserves size bytes; memory is NOT cleared; returns NULL on failure calloc(n, size) Reserves n x size bytes and sets all to zero realloc(ptr, size) Resizes a block (may move it); returns the new address free(ptr) Returns the block to the heap #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> int main(void) { int n = 5; int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof *arr); // space for 5 ints if (arr == NULL) { // ALWAYS check printf("Out of memory\n"); return 1; } for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = i * i; // grow to 10 elements: use a temporary pointer int *tmp = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof *arr); if (tmp == NULL) { free(arr); return 1; } arr = tmp; for (int i = 5; i < 10; i++) arr[i] = i * i; for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) printf("%d ", arr[i]); free(arr); // give it back arr = NULL; // avoid a dangling pointer return 0; } Output: 0 1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 Why sizeof *arr? It stays correct even if you change the pointer type later. Why a temporary pointer in realloc? If realloc fails it returns NULL, and writing that straight into arr would lose the old block (a leak).

title: 7.4 Linked list: a classic heap use
text: An array has a fixed size. A linked list grows one node at a time; each node holds data and a pointer to the next node. typedef struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; } Node; Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) { Node *n = malloc(sizeof *n); if (n == NULL) return head; n->data = value; n->next = head; // new node points to old first node return n; // new node is now the head } void print_list(const Node *head) { for (const Node *p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next) printf("%d -> ", p->data); printf("NULL\n"); } void free_list(Node *head) { while (head != NULL) { Node *next = head->next; // save before freeing free(head); head = next; } } int main(void) { Node *list = NULL; list = push_front(list, 3); list = push_front(list, 2); list = push_front(list, 1); print_list(list); free_list(list); return 0; } Output: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> NULL

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. Difference between malloc and calloc? calloc takes count and size and zeroes the memory; malloc does not initialise. Q2. What is a memory leak? Allocated memory that is never freed and can no longer be reached. Q3. What does realloc do if it cannot extend in place? It allocates a new block, copies the data and frees the old one. Q4. Why avoid malloc in embedded systems? Fragmentation, unpredictable timing and failure handling on tiny RAM. Q5. Stack vs heap? Stack is automatic and fast for locals; heap is manual and flexible for run-time sizes. Q6. What happens if you free the same pointer twice? Undefined behaviour, often a crash or heap corruption. title: 8.3 extern
text: extern says "this variable exists, it is defined in another file". It declares without creating. // config.c int baud_rate = 115200; // definition: memory is created here // main.c #include <stdio.h> extern int baud_rate; // declaration: refers to the one above int main(void) { printf("%d\n", baud_rate); return 0; } Normally you put the extern declaration in a header file (config.h) so every file shares the same one.

title: 8.6 Include guards
text: If two headers include the same header, the compiler sees duplicate definitions and fails. An include guard makes a header count only once. #ifndef SENSOR_H #define SENSOR_H int read_sensor(void); #endif

title: 8.7 Conditional compilation
text: #define DEBUG 1 #if DEBUG #define LOG(msg) printf("[LOG] %s\n", msg) #else #define LOG(msg) // expands to nothing in release builds #endif #ifdef ESP32 // code only for the ESP32 board #elif defined(ARDUINO_AVR_UNO) // code only for the Arduino Uno #endif Conditional compilation lets one code base support several boards or switch debug output on and off with zero cost in the final firmware.

title: File Handling

title: 9.1 Why files?
text: Variables vanish when the program ends. Files keep data: logs, configuration, records. On microcontrollers the same ideas apply to an SD card, SPIFFS or LittleFS on ESP32 (the function names differ slightly but the steps are the same). Analogy: a notebook Open the notebook (fopen), read or write on it (fprintf, fscanf, fread, fwrite), and close it (fclose) so everything is saved. title: 9.3 Text files

#include <stdio.h> int main(void) { FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "w"); if (fp == NULL) { perror("fopen"); // prints why it failed return 1; } fprintf(fp, "Ravi %d %.1f
", 101, 88.5); fprintf(fp, "Anu %d %.1f
", 102, 91.0); fclose(fp); fp = fopen("data.txt", "r"); if (fp == NULL) return 1; char name[20]; int roll; float marks; while (fscanf(fp, "%19s %d %f", name, &roll, &marks) == 3) printf("%s %d %.1f
", name, roll, marks); fclose(fp); return 0; } Output: Ravi 101 88.5 Anu 102 91.0 fscanf returns the number of items it managed to read. Looping while it returns 3 stops cleanly at the end of the file.

text: char line[100]; FILE *fp = fopen("log.txt", "r"); if (fp != NULL) { while (fgets(line, sizeof line, fp) != NULL) printf("%s", line); // fgets keeps the newline fclose(fp); } Function Use fprintf / fscanf Formatted text, like printf / scanf but for files fputs / fgets Write or read a line of text fputc / fgetc Write or read one character fwrite / fread Write or read raw bytes (binary files) fseek / ftell / rewind Move to a position, find the position, go back to start feof / ferror Check end of file or an error Function Use fprintf / fscanf Formatted text, like printf / scanf but for files fputs / fgets Write or read a line of text fputc / fgetc Write or read one character fwrite / fread Write or read raw bytes (binary files) fseek / ftell / rewind Move to a position, find the position, go back to start feof / ferror Check end of file or an error

title: 9.5 Binary files: save structs directly
text: typedef struct { char name[20]; int roll; float marks; } Student; Student s = {"Ravi", 101, 88.5f}; FILE *fp = fopen("students.bin", "wb"); if (fp) { fwrite(&s, sizeof(Student), 1, fp); // 1 record fclose(fp); } Student t; fp = fopen("students.bin", "rb"); if (fp) { if (fread(&t, sizeof(Student), 1, fp) == 1) printf("%s %d %.1f\n", t.name, t.roll, t.marks); fclose(fp); } Output: Ravi 101 88.5 Binary files are compact and fast, but they depend on the compiler, struct padding and endianness, so they are not portable between different systems. Text files are bigger but readable.

title: 9.6 Jumping around a file
text: fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); // go to the end long size = ftell(fp); // position = file size in bytes rewind(fp); // back to the start // jump straight to the 3rd record (index 2) of a binary file fseek(fp, 2 * sizeof(Student), SEEK_SET); The while(!feof(fp)) bug feof becomes true only after a read has failed, so this loop runs one extra time and processes garbage. title: Bitwise Operators and Bit Manipulation
text: In one line Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of a number. They are the main tool for controlling hardware registers, flags and protocols in embedded C. title: 10.1 Why bits matter in embedded
text: A hardware register is a number where each bit (or group of bits) controls one thing: bit 5 turns an LED pin on, bits 2 to 4 select a clock speed, bit 7 says "data ready". To change one bit without disturbing the others, you need bitwise operators. Analogy: a row of light switches A byte is a panel of 8 switches. Bitwise operators let you flip one switch, check one switch, or set a pattern, without touching the others. Analogy: a row of light switches A byte is a panel of 8 switches. Bitwise operators let you flip one switch, check one switch, or set a pattern, without touching the others.

Goal Code Why it works Set bit n x |= (1 << n); OR with a 1 forces the bit to 1, others unchanged Clear bit n x &= ~(1 << n); AND with a 0 forces the bit to 0, others unchanged Toggle bit n x ^= (1 << n); XOR with 1 flips the bit Check bit n if (x & (1 << n)) AND leaves only that bit; non-zero means it was 1 Goal Code Why it works Set bit n x |= (1 << n); OR with a 1 forces the bit to 1, others unchanged Clear bit n x &= ~(1 << n); AND with a 0 forces the bit to 0, others unchanged Toggle bit n x ^= (1 << n); XOR with 1 flips the bit Check bit n if (x & (1 << n)) AND leaves only that bit; non-zero means it was 1 Step by step: set bit 3 of x = 0b00000101 (5). #define SET_BIT(x, n) ((x) |= (1U << (n))) #define CLEAR_BIT(x, n) ((x) &= ~(1U << (n))) #define TOGGLE_BIT(x, n) ((x) ^= (1U << (n))) #define CHECK_BIT(x, n) (((x) >> (n)) & 1U) int main(void) { unsigned char x = 5; // 00000101 SET_BIT(x, 3); // 00001101 printf("%u

", x); // 12 TOGGLE_BIT(x, 7); // 10001100 printf("%u
", x); // 140 printf("%u

title: 10.4 Multi-bit fields: mask, shift, insert
text: Suppose bits 4 to 6 of a register hold a 3-bit "mode" value. #define MODE_SHIFT 4 #define MODE_MASK (0x7U << MODE_SHIFT) // 0111 0000 uint8_t reg = 0xA5; // 1010 0101 // READ the field: shift it down, then mask uint8_t mode = (reg >> MODE_SHIFT) & 0x7U; // 010 = 2 // WRITE the field: clear the old bits, then OR in the new value reg = (reg & ~MODE_MASK) | ((5U << MODE_SHIFT) & MODE_MASK); // mode = 101 This "clear then set" pattern is the standard way to update part of a register safely.

title: 10.5 Classic tricks (frequent interview questions)
text: // even or odd if (n & 1) { /* odd */ } // power of two (n must be > 0) int is_pow2 = (n > 0) && ((n & (n - 1)) == 0); // count set bits (Kernighan): each loop removes the lowest 1 bit int count_bits(unsigned int n) { int c = 0; while (n) { n &= (n - 1); c++; } return c; } // swap two numbers without a temporary variable a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; // swap the two nibbles of a byte uint8_t swapped = (uint8_t)((x << 4) | (x >> 4)); // multiply and divide by 8 (unsigned) y = x << 3; // x * 8 z = x >> 3; // x / 8 Why n & (n-1) works: subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 bit to 0 and all the zeros below it to 1, so AND-ing removes exactly that lowest 1.

title: 10.7 Real hardware example (Arduino Uno, AVR)
text: // Pin 13 on the Uno is PB5. Blink it with direct register access. void setup() { DDRB |= (1 << DDB5); // make PB5 an output } void loop() { PORTB ^= (1 << PORTB5); // toggle only PB5, other pins untouched delay(500); } DDRB is the direction register (1 = output). PORTB holds the output levels. One line toggles one pin and leaves the other seven alone. This is exactly why you learn bit manipulation.

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. How do you set, clear, toggle and check bit n? Set: x |= 1<<n. Clear: x &= ~(1<<n). Toggle: x ^= 1<<n. Check: (x>>n)&1. Q2. Difference between & and &&? & works on each bit; && works on whole values as true or false. Q3. How do you check for a power of 2? n > 0 and (n & (n-1)) == 0. Q4. What does x << n do? Shifts bits left by n places, equal to multiplying by 2^n if no overflow. Q5. How do you swap two variables without a temp? a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; (or with + and -). Q6. Why use unsigned for bit operations? Signed shifts and overflow have implementation-defined or undefined behaviour. Q7. How do you update a 3-bit field in a register without touching others? Clear the field with a mask, then OR in the new value shifted into position. TOPIC 11

title: Type Qualifiers and Fixed-Width Types
text: In one line volatile, const and static tell the compiler extra facts about a variable; fixed-width types (uint8_t, uint32_t...) make sizes identical on every chip. In one line volatile, const and static tell the compiler extra facts about a variable; fixed-width types (uint8_t, uint32_t...) make sizes identical on every chip.

title: 11.1 volatile
text: Compilers optimise. If your code reads a variable in a loop and nothing in that loop changes it, the compiler assumes it never changes and reads it only once. That is wrong if hardware or an interrupt changes it behind the compiler's back. volatile means: "this value can change at any time, always read it from memory and never cache it." Analogy: a whiteboard in a busy office Without volatile, the compiler copies the whiteboard into its notebook once and keeps reading its notes. With volatile, it must look at the whiteboard every single time, because someone else keeps writing on it. Analogy: a whiteboard in a busy office Without volatile, the compiler copies the whiteboard into its notebook once and keeps reading its notes. With volatile, it must look at the whiteboard every single time, because someone else keeps writing on it. int flag = 0; // BUG: not volatile void ISR(void) { flag = 1; } // interrupt sets the flag int main(void) { while (flag == 0) { } // compiler may turn this into an endless loop do_work(); } // FIX volatile int flag = 0; Three situations that need volatile: Situation Example Hardware register volatile uint32_t *status = (volatile uint32_t *)0x40021018; Variable changed in an ISR and read in main (or the reverse) volatile uint8_t button_pressed; Variable shared between tasks / threads (with proper locking) volatile bool running; Situation Example Hardware register volatile uint32_t *status = (volatile uint32_t *)0x40021018; Variable changed in an ISR and read in main (or the reverse) volatile uint8_t button_pressed; Variable shared between tasks / threads (with proper locking) volatile bool running; volatile does not make code safe volatile only stops the compiler from caching the value. It does not make a multi-byte read atomic. On an 8-bit AVR, reading a 16-bit volatile variable takes two instructions; an interrupt in between can give a half-old, half-new value. title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What does volatile do? It forbids the compiler from caching or removing reads and writes of that variable, because it may change outside the program flow. Q2. Give three uses of volatile in embedded systems. Hardware registers, ISR-shared variables, memory shared with DMA or other tasks. Q3. Can a variable be const and volatile? Why use uint8_t instead of unsigned char? Clear intent and a guaranteed 8-bit width. Q6. Where does const data live on a microcontroller? Usually in flash (read-only memory), which saves RAM. Q7. What is size_t? The unsigned type returned by sizeof, big enough to index any object. TOPIC 12

title: 12.3 What happens before main() runs
text: The CPU does not start at main. After power-on or reset it runs startup code: The linker script (.ld file) decides the addresses of flash and RAM and where each section goes. You rarely write it as a beginner, but you should know it exists. In Arduino and ESP-IDF these steps are hidden inside the core. Why interviewers ask this It shows you understand why a global initialised to 5 survives reset, why uninitialised globals are zero, and why local variables contain garbage. title: 12.5 Structure padding (recap with detail)
text: Processors prefer a 4-byte value at an address divisible by 4. The compiler adds padding to guarantee alignment. struct A { char a; int b; char c; }; // offsets: a=0, b=4, c=8, size 12 struct B { int b; char a; char c; }; // offsets: b=0, a=4, c=5, size 8 // remove padding (slower access, not portable, may fault on some CPUs) struct __attribute__((packed)) P { char a; int b; char c; }; // size 6 Packed structs are useful for matching a communication packet byte by byte, but unaligned access can be slow or even cause a hardware fault on some ARM cores. Prefer ordering members largest first.

title: 12.6 Endianness
text: A 32-bit number takes 4 bytes. Endianness is the order in which those bytes are stored. Little-endian Big-endian Stores first Least significant byte Most significant byte 0x12345678 in memory 78 56 34 12 12 34 56 78 Used by x86 PCs, ESP32, ESP8266, AVR, most ARM Cortex-M Network byte order, some old CPUs Little-endian Big-endian Stores first Least significant byte Most significant byte 0x12345678 in memory 78 56 34 12 12 34 56 78 Used by x86 PCs, ESP32, ESP8266, AVR, most ARM Cortex-M Network byte order, some old CPUs Analogy: writing a date Little-endian is like writing 29-10-2026 (small unit first). Big-endian is like 2026-10-29 (biggest unit first). Both hold the same date; both sides must agree on the order. Analogy: writing a date Little-endian is like writing 29-10-2026 (small unit first). Big-endian is like 2026-10-29 (biggest unit first). Both hold the same date; both sides must agree on the order. #include <stdio.h> #include <stdint.h> int main(void) { uint32_t x = 0x12345678; uint8_t *p = (uint8_t *)&x; // look at the first byte in memory if (*p == 0x78) printf("Little-endian\n"); else printf("Big-endian\n"); return 0; } Output: Little-endian Endianness matters when you send multi-byte values over UART, I2C, SPI or a network, or read a binary file made on another system. Convert explicitly, for example by sending the high byte first: tx[0] = (value >> 8) & 0xFF; tx[1] = value & 0xFF;

text: Q1. What are .text, .data and .bss? .text is code, .data is initialised globals, .bss is zero-initialised globals. Q2. Why are uninitialised globals zero? title: Registers, Memory-Mapped I/O and Function Pointers
text: In one line In a microcontroller, peripherals (GPIO, timers, UART) are controlled by writing numbers to special memory addresses called registers; C does this with volatile pointers to fixed addresses. In one line In a microcontroller, peripherals (GPIO, timers, UART) are controlled by writing numbers to special memory addresses called registers; C does this with volatile pointers to fixed addresses.

title: 13.1 What is a register?
text: A register is a small memory location, 8, 16 or 32 bits wide, that is connected to hardware instead of ordinary RAM. Writing to it changes hardware behaviour; reading it tells you the hardware state. Analogy: the control panel of a machine Every switch and gauge on the panel has a fixed position. Memory-mapped I/O means each switch and gauge has a fixed memory address. Writing to the address flips the switch; reading the address reads the gauge. Analogy: the control panel of a machine Every switch and gauge on the panel has a fixed position. Memory-mapped I/O means each switch and gauge has a fixed memory address. Writing to the address flips the switch; reading the address reads the gauge. Register type Purpose Control Configure the peripheral (enable it, set mode, pick speed) Status Hardware reports state (data ready, buffer empty, error) Data Hold the data to send or the data received Direction (GPIO) Choose input or output per pin Interrupt enable / flag Turn interrupts on and show which one fired Register type Purpose Control Configure the peripheral (enable it, set mode, pick speed) Status Hardware reports state (data ready, buffer empty, error) Data Hold the data to send or the data received Direction (GPIO) Choose input or output per pin Interrupt enable / flag Turn interrupts on and show which one fired

title: 13.2 Accessing a fixed address
text: The pattern is: cast the address to a pointer to volatile, then dereference. // NOTE: 0x40020014 is an example address. Real addresses come from // the chip's reference manual or its header file. #define GPIOA_ODR (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020014) GPIOA_ODR |= (1U << 5); // set pin 5 high GPIOA_ODR &= ~(1U << 5); // set pin 5 low GPIOA_ODR ^= (1U << 5); // toggle pin 5 Read the macro from the inside out: 0x40020014 is a number; (volatile uint32_t *) says "treat it as the address of a volatile 32-bit value"; the leading * says "the value at that address". The macro therefore behaves like a variable that is really hardware.

title: 13.3 Grouping registers in a struct
text: A peripheral usually has many registers in a row. A struct that matches the layout lets you name them (this is what vendor headers like STM32 CMSIS do). typedef struct { volatile uint32_t MODER; // offset 0x00 : pin mode (input/output) volatile uint32_t OTYPER; // offset 0x04 volatile uint32_t OSPEEDR; // offset 0x08 volatile uint32_t PUPDR; // offset 0x0C volatile uint32_t IDR; // offset 0x10 : input data volatile uint32_t ODR; // offset 0x14 : output data } GPIO_TypeDef; #define GPIOA ((GPIO_TypeDef *)0x40020000) GPIOA->MODER |= (1U << (5 * 2)); // pin 5 as output (2 bits per pin) GPIOA->ODR ^= (1U << 5); // toggle pin 5 if (GPIOA->IDR & (1U << 0)) { /* pin 0 is high */ }

title: 13.4 Practice safely: simulate a register on a PC
text: You can test all the bit logic without hardware by pointing at a normal variable. #include <stdio.h> #include <stdint.h> static volatile uint32_t fake_odr = 0; // pretend hardware register #define ODR (*(&fake_odr)) #define LED_PIN 5 int main(void) { ODR |= (1U << LED_PIN); // LED on printf("ODR = 0x%08X\n", (unsigned)ODR); ODR ^= (1U << LED_PIN); // toggle -> off printf("ODR = 0x%08X\n", (unsigned)ODR); return 0; } Output: ODR = 0x00000020 ODR = 0x00000000

title: 13.5 Read-modify-write and its risks
text: ODR |= mask looks like one operation, but the CPU does three: read the register, change the bits, write it back. If an interrupt changes the same register between the read and the write, its change is lost. Solutions: disable interrupts around it, or use hardware set and clear registers (BSRR on STM32, set/clear registers on ESP32 such as GPIO_OUT_W1TS and GPIO_OUT_W1TC) that change a bit with one write.

title: 13.6 Function pointers and callbacks
text: A function pointer stores the address of a function. Embedded software uses them to let low-level drivers call back into your application code. typedef void (*ButtonCallback)(void); static ButtonCallback on_press = NULL; void button_register(ButtonCallback cb) { // driver API on_press = cb; } void button_isr(void) { // driver calls your code if (on_press != NULL) on_press(); } void my_handler(void) { printf("Button pressed!\n"); } // application code int main(void) { button_register(my_handler); button_isr(); // simulate an interrupt return 0; } Output: Button pressed! The driver does not need to know what your application does, and your application does not need to know how the button is read. This separation is the heart of clean driver design.

title: 13.7 Table of function pointers (jump table)
text:
void cmd_on(void) { printf("LED on
"); } void cmd_off(void) { printf("LED off
"); } void cmd_blink(void) { printf("LED blink

title: GPIO and Debouncing
text: In one line GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) pins let the microcontroller read buttons and drive LEDs; debouncing removes the false presses caused by a mechanical switch's contacts bouncing. title: 14.1 What is a GPIO pin?
text: A pin you can configure in software as an input (read high or low) or an output (drive high or low). High means close to the supply voltage (3.3 V on ESP32 and ESP8266, 5 V on Arduino Uno); low means 0 V. Mode Meaning Input Pin listens. Reads 1 if voltage is high, 0 if low Input with pull-up Internal resistor pulls the pin to high when nothing drives it Input with pull-down Internal resistor pulls the pin to low when nothing drives it Output push-pull Pin actively drives both high and low (normal LED output) Output open-drain Pin can only pull low; a pull-up resistor makes high (I2C uses this) Mode Meaning Input Pin listens. title: 14.2 Floating inputs and pull-up resistors

title: 14.3 Output: driving an LED
text: const int LED_PIN = 2; void setup() { pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT); } void loop() { digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW); delay(500); } Always use a series resistor with an external LED. Example: supply 3.3 V, LED drop 2.0 V, wanted current 10 mA. R = (3.3 - 2.0) / 0.010 = 130 ohm. Use the next standard value, 150 or 220 ohm. Without a resistor the LED (or the pin) burns out.

title: 14.4 Input: reading a button
text: const int BTN_PIN = 4; const int LED_PIN = 2; void setup() { pinMode(BTN_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP); // pressed = LOW pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT); } void loop() { if (digitalRead(BTN_PIN) == LOW) // button pressed digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH); else digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW); }

title: 14.5 Switch bounce
text: A mechanical button is two pieces of metal. When they touch, they vibrate and make and break contact many times for about 1 to 20 milliseconds before settling. The microcontroller is fast enough to see every one of these as a separate press. What you do What the pin sees What your code may think One press HIGH, LOW, HIGH, LOW, HIGH, LOW (settles) 3 presses One release LOW, HIGH, LOW, HIGH (settles) 2 releases What you do What the pin sees What your code may think One press HIGH, LOW, HIGH, LOW, HIGH, LOW (settles) 3 presses One release LOW, HIGH, LOW, HIGH (settles) 2 releases The result: a counter that jumps by 3 or a toggle that flips randomly. Debouncing makes one physical press produce exactly one event.

title: 14.6 Software debouncing without blocking
text: The simple fix delay(20) after a press blocks the whole program. A better method: accept a new value only if it has stayed the same for a debounce time, using millis() for timing. const int BTN_PIN = 4; const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 30; int stableState = HIGH; // debounced state of the button int lastReading = HIGH; // raw reading from the previous loop unsigned long lastChange = 0; // when the raw reading last changed int pressCount = 0; void setup() { pinMode(BTN_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP); Serial.begin(115200); } void loop() { int reading = digitalRead(BTN_PIN); if (reading != lastReading) { // raw value changed: restart timer lastChange = millis(); lastReading = reading; } if ((millis() - lastChange) > DEBOUNCE_MS && reading != stableState) { stableState = reading; // it stayed stable long enough if (stableState == LOW) { // falling edge = real press pressCount++; Serial.println(pressCount); } } } The program stays free to do other work in loop() because nothing waits. The trick: millis() - lastChange measures how long the raw reading has stayed the same.

title: Interrupts and ISR

title: 15.1 Polling vs interrupts
text: Analogy: waiting for a visitor Polling is walking to the door every few seconds to see if someone is there. An interrupt is a doorbell: you work normally, and when it rings you go to the door, then return to your work. title: 15.2 What happens when an interrupt fires
text: The delay between the event and the first ISR instruction is the interrupt latency. Keeping ISRs short keeps latency for other interrupts low.

title: 15.3 The golden rules of an ISR
text: Rule Reason Keep it short and fast While an ISR runs, other work and (often) other interrupts wait No delay(), no waiting loops The timer that delay depends on may be blocked; the system freezes No printf or Serial.print They are slow, may use interrupts themselves and are not safe here No malloc / free Not re-entrant and unpredictable in time Do not call functions that block Anything that waits can hang the whole program Share data through volatile variables Otherwise the compiler may never see the change Set a flag or push data to a buffer, process in main Work in the ISR, think in main Rule Reason Keep it short and fast While an ISR runs, other work and (often) other interrupts wait No delay(), no waiting loops The timer that delay depends on may be blocked; the system freezes No printf or Serial.print They are slow, may use interrupts themselves and are not safe here No malloc / free Not re-entrant and unpredictable in time Do not call functions that block Anything that waits can hang the whole program Share data through volatile variables Otherwise the compiler may never see the change Set a flag or push data to a buffer, process in main Work in the ISR, think in main

title: 15.4 Example: button interrupt with a flag
text: const int BTN_PIN = 4; volatile bool buttonFlag = false; // shared with the ISR: volatile volatile unsigned long lastIsrTime = 0; void IRAM_ATTR onButton() { // ESP32: ISR must live in IRAM unsigned long now = millis(); if (now - lastIsrTime > 50) { // ignore bounces within 50 ms buttonFlag = true; // just set a flag lastIsrTime = now; } } void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); pinMode(BTN_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP); attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BTN_PIN), onButton, FALLING); } void loop() { if (buttonFlag) { // main code does the real work buttonFlag = false; Serial.println("Button pressed"); } // other tasks keep running here }

title: 15.5 Race conditions and atomic access
text: A race condition happens when main code and an ISR use the same data and the result depends on timing. Example of the problem An 8-bit AVR reads a 16-bit variable in two steps. If an interrupt changes the variable between the two reads, main gets the low byte of the old value and the high byte of the new value: a number that never existed. If an interrupt changes the variable between the two reads, main gets the low byte of the old value and the high byte of the new value: a number that never existed. volatile uint16_t pulseCount = 0; // incremented in an ISR uint16_t readCount(void) { noInterrupts(); // start critical section uint16_t copy = pulseCount; // read safely interrupts(); // end critical section return copy; } Keep critical sections as short as possible. On 32-bit chips a 32-bit read is a single instruction and is already atomic, but read-modify-write sequences like count++ still are not.

The handler function; keep it short, no blocking or printing, use volatile shared data. Q3. Why not call printf in an ISR? It is slow, may block and is not re-entrant. Q4. What is interrupt latency? title: Timers, PWM and ADC
text: In one line A timer counts clock ticks to measure and create precise time; PWM uses fast on-off switching to control power; an ADC converts a real-world voltage into a number. In one line A timer counts clock ticks to measure and create precise time; PWM uses fast on-off switching to control power; an ADC converts a real-world voltage into a number.

title: 16.1 Timers
text: A hardware timer is a counter that increases by one on every tick of a clock, completely independent of your program. It can raise an interrupt on overflow or when it reaches a chosen compare value. Analogy: a kitchen timer You set the number of minutes, go on cooking, and it rings at the right time. A hardware timer keeps counting while the CPU does other jobs. Analogy: a kitchen timer You set the number of minutes, go on cooking, and it rings at the right time. A hardware timer keeps counting while the CPU does other jobs. Key terms: How to calculate a period, step by step (Uno: 16 MHz clock, want 1 ms): // Arduino Uno: Timer2 generates an interrupt every 1 ms volatile unsigned long ms = 0; void setup() { noInterrupts(); TCCR2A = (1 << WGM21); // CTC mode: clear counter on match TCCR2B = (1 << CS22); // prescaler 64 OCR2A = 249; // compare value TIMSK2 = (1 << OCIE2A); // enable compare-match interrupt interrupts(); } ISR(TIMER2_COMPA_vect) { ms++; // runs every 1 ms } void loop() { // use ms as a millisecond clock here } This register-level code is for the Uno (AVR). Using Timer2 leaves Timer0 free for millis() and delay(), but tone() also uses Timer2. On ESP32 and ESP8266 the timer API differs between core versions, so check the documentation of the core you installed. The calculation is the same on every chip.

title: 16.2 Non-blocking timing with millis()
text: unsigned long previous = 0; const unsigned long INTERVAL = 1000; // 1 second bool ledOn = false; void loop() { unsigned long now = millis(); if (now - previous >= INTERVAL) { // subtraction is safe when millis() wraps previous = now; ledOn = !ledOn; digitalWrite(2, ledOn); } // loop keeps running: read sensors, check buttons... }

title: 16.3 PWM: Pulse Width Modulation
text: PWM switches a pin on and off very fast. The fraction of time it is ON is the duty cycle. A load that cannot follow such fast changes (an LED to the eye, a motor with inertia) sees the average. Duty cycle Average voltage (3.3 V) Effect 0% 0 V Always off 25% 0.83 V Dim LED, slow motor 50% 1.65 V Half brightness or speed 75% 2.48 V Bright 100% 3.3 V Always on Duty cycle Average voltage (3.3 V) Effect 0% 0 V Always off 25% 0.83 V Dim LED, slow motor 50% 1.65 V Half brightness or speed 75% 2.48 V Bright 100% 3.3 V Always on // Arduino Uno: fade an LED on pin 9 int brightness = 0; int step = 5; void setup() { pinMode(9, OUTPUT); } void loop() { analogWrite(9, brightness); // 0 = off, 255 = full brightness += step; if (brightness <= 0 || brightness >= 255) step = -step; delay(20); } Servo motors use a specific PWM: 50 Hz (20 ms period) with a pulse of 1 ms (one end), 1.5 ms (centre) and 2 ms (other end). Use a Servo library so the timing is exact.

title: Communication Protocols: UART, I2C and SPI
text: In one line Protocols are agreed rules for sending bytes between chips: UART is a simple two-wire serial link, I2C connects many devices on two shared wires, and SPI is a fast four-wire link. In one line Protocols are agreed rules for sending bytes between chips: UART is a simple two-wire serial link, I2C connects many devices on two shared wires, and SPI is a fast four-wire link.

title: 17.1 Serial vs parallel, sync vs async
17.2 UART
text: UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter) connects exactly two devices. It is what the Serial Monitor, GPS modules, Bluetooth modules (HC-05) and many sensors use. Wire Connection TX Transmit of device A goes to RX of device B RX Receive of device A comes from TX of device B (so TX and RX are crossed) GND Common ground is mandatory Wire Connection TX Transmit of device A goes to RX of device B RX Receive of device A comes from TX of device B (so TX and RX are crossed) GND Common ground is mandatory Frame format 8N1 (the most common): when idle the line is HIGH. One byte is sent as: 1 start bit (LOW), 8 data bits (least significant bit first), no parity, 1 stop bit (HIGH). That is 10 bits for 8 bits of data. void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); // must match the Serial Monitor } void loop() { if (Serial.available() > 0) { // a byte has arrived char c = Serial.read(); Serial.print("Got: "); Serial.println(c); } } Receiving commands properly: build a line in a buffer until you see a newline, then parse it. Check buffer length so a long message cannot overflow it. char line[32]; uint8_t len = 0; void loop() { while (Serial.available() > 0) { char c = Serial.read(); if (c == '\n') { line[len] = '\0'; handle_command(line); // e.g. compare with strcmp len = 0; } else if (len < sizeof(line) - 1) { line[len++] = c; // protect against overflow } } }

title: 17.3 I2C
text: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit, "I squared C") uses just two shared wires for many devices: SDA (data) and SCL (clock). One master (your microcontroller) talks to several slaves (sensors, displays, EEPROM). Each slave has a 7-bit address. Analogy: a classroom The teacher (master) calls a student by name (the address) and asks a question. Only the student whose name was called answers. Everyone shares the same room (the two wires). Analogy: a classroom The teacher (master) calls a student by name (the address) and asks a question. Only the student whose name was called answers. Everyone shares the same room (the two wires). // I2C scanner: finds the addresses of all connected devices #include <Wire.h> void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); Wire.begin(); for (uint8_t addr = 1; addr < 127; addr++) { Wire.beginTransmission(addr); if (Wire.endTransmission() == 0) { // 0 = device answered (ACK) Serial.print("Found device at 0x"); Serial.println(addr, HEX); } } } void loop() {} // Read two bytes from a sensor register (generic pattern) Wire.beginTransmission(0x48); // device address Wire.write(0x00); // register to read Wire.endTransmission(); Wire.requestFrom(0x48, 2); // ask for 2 bytes if (Wire.available() >= 2) { uint8_t hi = Wire.read(); uint8_t lo = Wire.read(); int16_t raw = (hi << 8) | lo; // combine: byte order from the datasheet } Typical I2C devices: OLED SSD1306 (0x3C), MPU6050 (0x68), BMP280 (0x76 or 0x77), RTC DS3231 (0x68), LCD backpack (0x27 or 0x3F). A common error: SDA and SCL swapped or missing pull-ups, so the scanner finds nothing.

title: 17.4 SPI
text: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is fast and simple: one master and one or more slaves. Data goes in both directions at the same time (full duplex). Wire Meaning SCK Clock from the master MOSI Master Out, Slave In: data from master to slave MISO Master In, Slave Out: data from slave to master CS (SS) Chip Select, one per slave; pull LOW to talk to that slave Wire Meaning SCK Clock from the master MOSI Master Out, Slave In: data from master to slave MISO Master In, Slave Out: data from slave to master CS (SS) Chip Select, one per slave; pull LOW to talk to that slave #include <SPI.h> const int CS_PIN = 5; void setup() { pinMode(CS_PIN, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(CS_PIN, HIGH); // idle: slave not selected SPI.begin(); } uint8_t spiReadRegister(uint8_t reg) { SPI.beginTransaction(SPISettings(1000000, MSBFIRST, SPI_MODE0)); digitalWrite(CS_PIN, LOW); // select the slave SPI.transfer(reg | 0x80); // send register address (read flag is device specific) uint8_t value = SPI.transfer(0x00); // send dummy byte, get the answer digitalWrite(CS_PIN, HIGH); // release the slave SPI.endTransaction(); return value; }

title: 17.5 Comparison
text: UART I2C SPI Wires 2 (TX, RX) + GND 2 shared (SDA, SCL) 3 + one CS per slave Devices 2 Many (addresses) Many (CS lines) Clock None (baud rate) Master clock Master clock Speed Up to about 1 Mbps 100 kHz to 400 kHz (up to MHz) 10 MHz and more Direction Full duplex Half duplex Full duplex Best for PC link, GPS, modules Sensors, small displays, RTC SD card, fast displays, flash UART I2C SPI Wires 2 (TX, RX) + GND 2 shared (SDA, SCL) 3 + one CS per slave Devices 2 Many (addresses) Many (CS lines) Clock None (baud rate) Master clock Master clock Speed Up to about 1 Mbps 100 kHz to 400 kHz (up to MHz) 10 MHz and more Direction Full duplex Half duplex Full duplex Best for PC link, GPS, modules Sensors, small displays, RTC SD card, fast displays, flash Quick rule: need to talk to a PC or a module with a serial port, use UART; many slow sensors on few pins, use I2C; high data rate, use SPI.

title: 17.6 Multi-byte values and byte order
text: A 16-bit sensor value arrives as two bytes. The datasheet says which byte comes first. Combine as (high << 8) | low if the high byte arrives first. Mixing this up is a very common bug (see endianness in Topic 12).

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is baud rate? The number of symbols (bits) sent per second on a serial line. Q2. What does 8N1 mean? 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. Q3. Why does I2C need pull-up resistors? The lines are open-drain, so devices can only pull them low; resistors pull them high. Q4. How many devices can an I2C bus have? Up to 112 usable 7-bit addresses in theory, fewer in practice because of capacitance and address clashes. Q5. What are MOSI, MISO, SCK and CS? text: In one line These are the reusable building blocks of real firmware: a ring buffer to pass data safely, a state machine to organise behaviour, a watchdog to recover from hangs, sleep modes to save power and an RTOS to run several tasks. title: 18.1 Circular (ring) buffer
text: A fixed-size buffer that wraps around. New data is written at the head; old data is read from the tail. Both indexes wrap to 0 when they reach the end. It is used for UART receive data, sensor samples and logging. Analogy: a circular conveyor belt One person puts items on the belt (head), another takes them off (tail). The belt never ends, it loops. If the putter is faster than the taker for too long, the belt fills up (overflow). Analogy: a circular conveyor belt One person puts items on the belt (head), another takes them off (tail). The belt never ends, it loops. If the putter is faster than the taker for too long, the belt fills up (overflow). #include <stdint.h> #include <stdbool.h> #define BUF_SIZE 8 // use a power of 2 so we can wrap with a mask typedef struct { uint8_t data[BUF_SIZE]; volatile uint8_t head; // written by the producer (ISR) volatile uint8_t tail; // written by the consumer (main) } RingBuffer; bool rb_is_empty(const RingBuffer *rb) { return rb->head == rb->tail; } bool rb_is_full (const RingBuffer *rb) { return ((rb->head + 1) & (BUF_SIZE - 1)) == rb->tail; // one slot stays empty } bool rb_put(RingBuffer *rb, uint8_t byte) { if (rb_is_full(rb)) return false; // overflow: report it rb->data[rb->head] = byte; rb->head = (rb->head + 1) & (BUF_SIZE - 1); // wrap: same as % 8 return true; } bool rb_get(RingBuffer *rb, uint8_t *byte) { if (rb_is_empty(rb)) return false; *byte = rb->data[rb->tail]; rb->tail = (rb->tail + 1) & (BUF_SIZE - 1); return true; } Typical use: the UART receive ISR calls rb_put for each byte; loop() calls rb_get and processes whatever has arrived.

title: 18.2 Finite state machine (FSM)
text: Many devices behave differently depending on what they are doing: waiting, running, error. A state machine keeps a variable for the current state and decides what to do next from the state and the event. It replaces tangled if-else flags with clear, testable logic. Current state Event Action Next state RED Timer (10 s) Turn red off, green on GREEN GREEN Timer (10 s) Turn green off, yellow on YELLOW YELLOW Timer (3 s) Turn yellow off, red on RED Current state Event Action Next state RED Timer (10 s) Turn red off, green on GREEN GREEN Timer (10 s) Turn green off, yellow on YELLOW YELLOW Timer (3 s) Turn yellow off, red on RED typedef enum { STATE_RED, STATE_GREEN, STATE_YELLOW } State; State state = STATE_RED; unsigned long stateStart = 0; void setLights(bool r, bool y, bool g) { digitalWrite(RED_PIN, r); digitalWrite(YELLOW_PIN, y); digitalWrite(GREEN_PIN, g); } void loop() { unsigned long now = millis(); switch (state) { case STATE_RED: setLights(1, 0, 0); if (now - stateStart >= 10000) { state = STATE_GREEN; stateStart = now; } break; case STATE_GREEN: setLights(0, 0, 1); if (now - stateStart >= 10000) { state = STATE_YELLOW; stateStart = now; } break; case STATE_YELLOW: setLights(0, 1, 0); if (now - stateStart >= 3000) { state = STATE_RED; stateStart = now; } break; } } You already built a traffic signal project; rebuilding it as an explicit state machine is a very good interview story.

title: 18.3 Watchdog timer
text: A watchdog is a hardware timer that resets the chip if your software does not "kick" (reset) it within a set time. If the code hangs in an infinite loop or crashes, the watchdog restarts the device automatically. Analogy: a dead-man's switch A train driver must press a pedal every few seconds. If the driver stops pressing, the train brakes automatically. The watchdog is the pedal; the reset is the brake. Analogy: a dead-man's switch A train driver must press a pedal every few seconds. If the driver stops pressing, the train brakes automatically. The watchdog is the pedal; the reset is the brake. // Arduino Uno (AVR) #include <avr/wdt.h> void setup() { wdt_enable(WDTO_2S); // reset if not kicked within 2 seconds } void loop() { do_work(); wdt_reset(); // kick the watchdog: "I am still alive" }

title: 18.4 Low-power and sleep modes

title: 18.5 Introduction to an RTOS
text: A Real-Time Operating System lets you write several independent tasks (read sensor, update display, handle Wi-Fi) that appear to run at the same time. A scheduler switches between them. The ESP32 Arduino core already runs on FreeRTOS, and your loop() is one task. Term Meaning Task An independent function with its own stack and priority Scheduler Decides which task runs, usually the highest priority one that is ready Delay vTaskDelay lets other tasks run while this one waits (unlike delay-busy waiting) Queue Thread-safe way to pass data between tasks or from an ISR to a task Semaphore / Mutex Signals an event or protects a shared resource from two tasks at once Term Meaning Task An independent function with its own stack and priority Scheduler Decides which task runs, usually the highest priority one that is ready Delay vTaskDelay lets other tasks run while this one waits (unlike delay-busy waiting) Queue Thread-safe way to pass data between tasks or from an ISR to a task Semaphore / Mutex Signals an event or protects a shared resource from two tasks at once // ESP32 (Arduino core): two tasks void blinkTask(void *param) { pinMode(2, OUTPUT); while (true) { digitalWrite(2, !digitalRead(2)); vTaskDelay(500 / portTICK_PERIOD_MS); // sleep 500 ms, others run } } void sensorTask(void *param) { while (true) { int v = analogRead(34); Serial.println(v); vTaskDelay(1000 / portTICK_PERIOD_MS); } } void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); xTaskCreate(blinkTask, "blink", 2048, NULL, 1, NULL); // name, stack bytes, param, priority, handle xTaskCreate(sensorTask, "sensor", 4096, NULL, 1, NULL); } void loop() {}

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is a circular buffer and where is it used? A fixed-size FIFO that wraps around; used for UART data, sensor streams and logs. Q2. How do you tell a full buffer from an empty one? Empty when head equals tail; full when head + 1 equals tail (one slot kept free), or use a count variable. Q3. What is a finite state machine? A model with a finite set of states and rules that move between them when events occur. Q4. What is a watchdog timer? A hardware timer that resets the system if the software fails to reset it in time. Q5. Why should you not kick the watchdog from an ISR? The ISR can keep running while main is stuck, hiding the hang. Q6. What is the difference between light sleep and deep sleep? Light sleep stops the CPU but keeps RAM and quick wake; deep sleep powers down almost everything for the lowest current but restarts the program. Q7. Super-loop vs RTOS? A super-loop is one endless loop (simple); an RTOS schedules several tasks with priorities and timing guarantees. Q8. What is a mutex? A lock that lets only one task use a shared resource at a time.

title: 1. What is a data type?
text: A data type tells the computer three things about a variable: Analogy: boxes and labels Think of memory as a warehouse full of boxes. A data type is the box size plus a label on the box. int is a medium box labelled "whole numbers only". char is a tiny box labelled "one character". double is a big box labelled "very precise decimal numbers". Without the label, the same contents can mean different things: the bits 01000001 can be the number 65 or the letter A. The data type decides how they are read. title: 3. The int data type in detail
3.1 What is int?
text: int is short for integer. It stores whole numbers: positive, negative or zero, with no decimal point. Examples: 0, 25, -400, 100000. Use int for things you count: number of students, loop counters, marks, age, array index. int students = 60; int temperature = -5; int total = students * 2; printf("Students = %d\n", students); // %d prints an int scanf("%d", &students); // %d reads an int (note the &) Remember %d is the format specifier for int. Using the wrong one (for example %f for an int) prints garbage. Remember %d is the format specifier for int. Using the wrong one (for example %f for an int) prints garbage.

title: 3.6 Overflow: when the number does not fit
text: Analogy: the car odometer A 3-digit odometer shows 999. Drive one more kilometre and it rolls over to 000. A fixed number of bits behaves the same way: after the maximum value it wraps around. Analogy: the car odometer A 3-digit odometer shows 999. Drive one more kilometre and it rolls over to 000. A fixed number of bits behaves the same way: after the maximum value it wraps around. Unsigned overflow is well defined in C: the value wraps around (modulo 2^n). unsigned char x = 255; x = x + 1; printf("%d\n", x); // 0 unsigned char y = 0; y = y - 1; printf("%d\n", y); // 255 Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C. It often wraps around in practice, but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so your program can behave strangely. Never rely on it. int a = INT_MAX; a = a + 1; // undefined behaviour: do not do this Real example: factorial overflows quickly with 32-bit int. Embedded example millis() on Arduino returns an unsigned 32-bit counter that wraps to 0 after about 49.7 days. Code that compares times as (now - start) >= interval keeps working across the wrap, because unsigned subtraction also wraps correctly. title: 3.9 Mixing int with other types
text: When you mix types in one expression, C converts them automatically (implicit conversion). Two rules cause most bugs: int a = -1; unsigned int b = 1; if (a < b) printf("a is smaller\n"); else printf("b is smaller\n"); // this prints! Why? -1 is converted to unsigned, which becomes 4,294,967,295, bigger than 1. This is one of the most common hidden bugs. Avoid comparing signed and unsigned values. Type casting changes a type on purpose: int total = 7, count = 2; float avg = (float)total / count; // 3.5, cast BEFORE dividing int x = (int)3.99; // 3, decimals are cut, not rounded

title: Interview questions with short answers
text: Q1. What is the size of int in C? It depends on the compiler and the processor. At least 16 bits by the standard; 32 bits on most modern systems (PC, ESP32, ARM), 16 bits on 8-bit AVR (Arduino Uno). Q2. What is the range of a 32-bit signed int? -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, which is -2^31 to 2^31 - 1. Q3. How are negative numbers stored? In two's complement: invert all bits of the positive number and add 1. The left-most bit acts as the sign bit. Q4. Difference between signed and unsigned int? Signed can hold negative values; unsigned cannot but has twice the positive range. Q5. What happens on integer overflow? Unsigned wraps around (modulo 2^n). Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. Q6. What is the result of 7 / 2 in C? 3, because both operands are int and the decimal part is truncated. Q7. What is the result of -7 % 2? -1. The sign of the remainder follows the left operand (since C99). Q8. Why use uint8_t instead of unsigned char or int in embedded code? Its size is guaranteed (exactly 8 bits), so the code behaves the same on every chip, and it clearly shows the data is a raw byte. Q9. What does this print: int a = -1; unsigned int b = 1; printf("%d", a < b); 0, because a is converted to unsigned (4,294,967,295) and the comparison is false. Q10. What is the difference between int x = 012 and int x = 12? 012 is octal and equals 10; 12 is decimal and equals 12.
